blocks.text: Chapter 5.
The Psychology of Human Misjudgment I: Incentives to Deprival

Tonight the locked trunk opens, friend. Charlie's masterwork — the catalog of the twenty-five standard ways the human mind fools itself. We take the first fourteen, and we start with a mystery at an airport in the middle of the night.

Federal Express's whole business rests on one promise: every package, moved between planes in the dark, sorted and out by dawn. And the night hub kept failing. Management tried everything — pleading, threatening, retraining. Nothing worked. The packages just wouldn't get sorted on time.

Pause and guess: No amount of moral pressure, supervision, or training fixed the FedEx night shift. Then management changed ONE thing — and the problem vanished essentially overnight. Around the same era, Xerox's founder Joe Wilson came back from government service to solve a twin mystery: an INFERIOR old machine was outselling his better new one. Same root cause. What was it?
Ready? Here is what happened.

The incentives — always the incentives, friend. FedEx was paying night workers by the hour: finishing early meant earning less, so the shift had every reason to stretch. Management switched to pay by the shift — done sorting, go home — and the packages flew through. At Xerox, salesmen earned higher commissions on the worse machine, so the worse machine sold. This is Charlie's Tendency One: reward and punishment superresponse — the most powerful, most underrated force in human affairs; almost nothing predicts behavior as reliably. And its most dangerous child is incentive-caused bias: a decent person's thinking drifts, without a flicker of conscious dishonesty, toward whatever serves his interests — the surgeon removing healthy gall bladders sincerely believing they're diseased; the consultant whose every report recommends more consulting. So Charlie's rules: fear professional advice that's especially good for the adviser; appeal to interest, never to reason, when you'd persuade (that's Franklin); design systems that make cheating hard — the humble cash register, he says, did more for morality than any sermon — and never sign a cost-plus contract without knowing exactly what you're inviting. Punishment works too: Rome had the bridge's builder stand beneath the arch while the scaffolding came out. Accountability, friend, concentrates the engineering mind wonderfully.
The heart's thumbs on the scale

The next tendencies work through raw feeling, friend — and all of them below the level where you can watch them operate. Liking makes you ignore the faults of people you love, and favor anything merely associated with them — which is exactly why advertisers hire beautiful, likable faces. Hating is its mirror: you ignore the virtues of those you dislike and bend facts to feed the grudge — at war strength it makes whole nations believe anything about an enemy; at office strength it quietly corrupts every dispute. And then there's envy — Charlie's special contempt. Buffett's line: it's envy, not greed, that drives the world — people tolerate being poor far more easily than being poorer than a neighbor. One salary leak can wreck a sensible institution. And yet, Charlie marvels, envy is nearly absent from the psychology textbooks — too taboo to name, too costly to ignore.

Then comes the rush to certainty. The brain hates doubt — a threatened animal can't afford long deliberation — so under puzzlement plus stress it grabs any conclusion fast; that's why courts force judges and juries to wait for the evidence, and why you should wait too when nothing's chasing you. Worse is inconsistency-avoidance: once a conclusion is in, the mind seals like an egg after one sperm enters — first-conclusion bias. Keynes noticed it in the most educated men alive: the hard part was never accepting new ideas, but escaping old ones. This machinery has a bright exploit and a dark one, friend. Bright: Franklin turned a hostile legislator into a lifelong ally by asking to borrow a rare book — the man reasoned backward from his own favor and decided he must like Franklin. Dark: hazing and painful initiations make recruits value the group more, because admitting the suffering was pointless is intolerable — cults run on it. So be slow to pound in your own conclusions... and keep curiosity burning, because it's one of the few native forces that undoes the rest.

Pause and guess: Now the social reflexes manipulators love. Robert Cialdini's researchers asked students to chaperone a group of juvenile delinquents on a zoo trip. One in six said yes. Then, with fresh students, they changed the approach with a single trick — and compliance TRIPLED to one in two. Nothing about the zoo trip changed. What was the trick?
Ready? Here is what happened.

They asked for something outrageous first. Two years of weekly counseling — refused, of course. Then they "retreated" to the little zoo trip... and the students, feeling the requester had made a concession, felt compelled to concede back. That's reciprocation tendency, friend — we return favors AND disfavors, often with interest, and a manufactured concession is a favor your brain repays automatically. It's the car salesman's free coffee, the vendor's lunch that quietly corrupts a purchasing agent — Sam Walton banned his buyers from accepting so much as a sandwich, because he'd read the mechanism correctly. (Its noble side underwrites trade, marriage, and the spontaneous Christmas truces of the World War One trenches; guilt, Charlie says, is what you feel when the repay-the-favor program collides with your incentives.) Its cousin is Kantian fairness — strangers alternating politely at highway merges with no policeman in sight — and its violation breeds disproportionate, lasting rage. And mere association extends Pavlov everywhere: buyers infer quality from price alone — raise the price, sometimes sales go UP; past success under certain conditions convinces a man the conditions caused the wins. Nastiest of all: Persian messenger syndrome — hating the bearer of bad news, as ancient kings killed messengers and as CBS decayed once Bill Paley's subordinates learned to bring only sunshine. The antidote is a standing culture of bad news first — and rewarding, visibly, the next person who brings it.
The flattering mirror

Two tendencies keep the self-portrait retouched, friend. Denial distorts reality until it's bearable — Charlie tells of a family friend who insisted her athlete son, lost at sea, was still alive. In grief, forgivable. In addiction, fatal: the alcoholic denies the deterioration precisely when clear sight matters most — which is why Charlie's rule on addictive chemicals is absolute avoidance; denial disables the alarm exactly when it should ring.

Excessive self-regard is sneakier. Ninety percent of Swedish drivers rate themselves above average. People overvalue what they own — the endowment effect — and, crucially, they own their conclusions too, which supercharges first-conclusion bias. Lottery players pay more for tickets with self-picked numbers, though the odds never move. Hiring committees swoon over vivid interviews and ignore boring, predictive track records — trust the record, Charlie says, not the performance in the chair. And self-regard writes generous moral accounting: the Tolstoy effect — the worst criminals don't think they're bad; they deny the crime, or excuse it as understandable. Institutions must tolerate neither move — Charlie admires the Navy's rule that the captain whose ship runs aground is finished, fair or not, because the unforgiving standard protects everyone. The working antidote: treat your own opinions with a stranger's skepticism. The easiest person for you to fool, friend, is you.
Wishing, and the bite of loss

Overoptimism needs no pain to trigger it — Demosthenes had it twenty-three centuries ago: "What a man wishes, that also will he believe." The cure isn't a mood; it's a method — force every wish through the arithmetic of Fermat and Pascal.

And the fourteenth tendency, friend, you've already met twice on this shelf. The Munger family dog was a sweet, agreeable animal — with one exception. Try to take food out of its mouth, and it would bite the hand that fed it. Deprival superreaction: losses — and even near-misses of gains — hurt far more than equivalent gains please. Slot machines are engineered around it: shower the player with near-misses, each one screaming you almost had it, each one buying another coin. Labor unions destroyed the very employers who fed them rather than accept takebacks — surrendering what workers already had felt unbearable even when refusal meant losing everything. And New Coke? A deprival lollapalooza: taking away the sacred flavor read, in a hundred million brains, as theft. The antidotes: evaluate every position as if starting fresh — ignore what you paid, ignore what you almost had. And Charlie's auction rule is pure gold, friend: the best defense against a stupid bidding war is not attending.
Before you go

Fourteen down, friend: incentives rule everything (fix the system before blaming the people); liking, hating, and envy bend facts silently; the mind seals on first conclusions — stay curious and slow to commit; reciprocation, fairness, and association are reflexes salesmen play like instruments — bad news first, always; the mirror flatters — trust records over interviews and never excuse yourself twice; wishes corrupt probabilities, and losses bite like the old dog. This week: before judging any advice or failure, write down who gets paid for what — then ask if the conclusion survives a change in incentives.

But Charlie isn't done with the trunk. Eleven tendencies remain — and they include the strongest of them all: the one that makes a whole crowd wrong together, the reason teenagers, mobs, and markets move as one. And at the very end, the grand finale — what happens when several tendencies fire at once: the lollapalooza that makes a Tupperware party irresistible and an open-outcry auction a machine for ruin. Next time: social proof to lollapaloozas.
Key takeaways
Tendency #1 rules them all: reward/punishment superresponse — FedEx fixed its night hub by paying by the shift, not the hour; fix incentives before blaming people.
Incentive-caused bias corrupts honestly: fear advice that's especially good for the adviser, and appeal to interest, not reason.
The mind seals on first conclusions like an egg; escaping old ideas is harder than accepting new ones — curiosity and deliberate opposite-arguing are the antidotes.
Reciprocation is exploitable at will: Cialdini's fake concession tripled compliance; Walton banned vendor lunches for a reason — and insist on bad news first.
The mirror flatters: 90% of drivers are "above average," conclusions become possessions, and criminals excuse themselves — trust track records over interviews.
Losses hurt ~twice as much as gains please: near-misses power slot machines, deprival killed New Coke — evaluate afresh, and skip the auction entirely.
